extracted.intended_audience: companies, marketers, individuals, and in-house or outside counsel facing or seeking to avoid FTC allegations of false or deceptive advertising
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what the FTC considers false or deceptive advertising, examples of problematic practices, the FTC's investigatory powers and risks, and practical defensive/compliance measures for advertisers and their counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 'false' and 'deceptive' advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: As the FTC makes clear, 'false' and 'deceptive' do not mean the same thing; an advertisement can be false, deceptive, or both. Both present equal risks and carry the same penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding the difference is important for formulating a targeted defense strategy because the legal bases, evidence, and defenses may differ even though penalties are similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: False advertising — disprovable/patently untrue claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The FTC will consider an advertisement to be 'false' if it can be disproven — i.e., if it is patently and objectively untrue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written language that misrepresents a product’s quality or capabilities (durability, components, ingredients, reliability, effectiveness) can be false. Example anti-patterns: claiming a product does things it does not; pharmaceutical claims that drugs treat conditions when they do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: False advertising — claims that cannot be proven (lack of substantiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: An advertisement can also be deemed false if it cannot be proven to be true, including self-aggrandizing claims or statements lacking substantiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: claiming a product is 'Consumers’ preferred choice' without conducting a scientific survey is considered false for enforcement purposes. Advertisers must have documentation to support substantive claims; even true claims can trigger enforcement if the advertiser cannot prove them during an investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Images and video can constitute false advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Images and videos that show a product doing something the product is not actually capable of doing constitute false advertising even if no written claims accompany them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual representations are treated like affirmative claims; ensure demonstrations are authentic and reflect typical consumer experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceptive advertising — omission of material information
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements can be deceptive because they exclude information that is material to consumers’ purchasing decisions, not only because they make affirmative false statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When advertisers know favorable and unfavorable information, selectively publishing or omitting material facts can be deceptive. Defense requires identifying what omissions are alleged and whether omitted facts are material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceptive tactic — publishing only favorable reviews or testimonials
rubrics_metrics.description: Only publishing a company’s five-star reviews or promoting testimonials while attempting to bury legitimate complaints can constitute deceptive advertising under the FTC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies should avoid presenting an unbalanced portrait of consumer opinion when using reviews or testimonials in advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceptive tactic — selectively publishing test or survey results
rubrics_metrics.description: Selectively publishing test or survey results (e.g., reporting that most customers find a product effective while ignoring significant reports of unreliability) can lead to allegations of deceptive advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports and survey summaries used in marketing should be representative and not omit adverse results that would be material to consumers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deceptive tactic — omitting required disclosures (endorsements & affiliates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Omitting necessary disclosures (for example, when using brand ambassadors or affiliate marketers) can render advertising deceptive; companies and endorsers must ensure compliance with the FTC’s Endorsement Guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmative disclosures are often required; both the company and endorsers/affiliates share responsibility for compliance with endorsement/disclosure rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example of deceptive omission/context (misleading credentials/events)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting an event or credential without material context can be deceptive — e.g., claiming to have 'spoken at Harvard' when the presenter paid to record a commercial on school grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid implying endorsements, credentials, or contexts that materially mislead consumers; disclose material contextual facts when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centrality of substantiation to FTC liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Many false/deceptive advertising cases hinge on whether the advertiser can substantiate its claims; substantiation often determines whether the FTC will pursue enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers should document tests, surveys, and other evidence supporting claims before publishing; lack of adequate substantiation can result in civil enforcement even absent intentional falsity.

rubrics_metrics.name: FTC investigatory and enforcement authorities (risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: The FTC has authority to issue civil investigative demands (CIDs) and subpoenas and to impose fines, injunctions, and other penalties; intentional fraud findings can lead to DOJ criminal referral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facing an FTC investigation is a serious matter — potential consequences include monetary penalties, injunctive relief, and possible criminal referral. Awareness of risks should drive proactive compliance and defense planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: FTC investigative techniques and compulsory process
rubrics_metrics.description: The FTC conducts market surveillance, interviews employees and partners, works with whistleblowers, and can issue judicially enforceable CIDs and administrative subpoenas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-compliance with CIDs/subpoenas can lead to enforcement regardless of the underlying allegation’s merit; timely, strategic responses are required when process arrives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended defensive posture and tactics
rubrics_metrics.description: To defend against FTC allegations, engage experienced defense counsel promptly, present a coordinated strategic defense, comply appropriately with CIDs/subpoenas while preserving defenses and attorney-client privilege, and consider settlement when substantiation is weak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps: retain counsel immediately, inventory and preserve documentation supporting claims, avoid self-incriminating disclosures, evaluate settlement vs litigation strategy, and ensure communications with endorsers/affiliates satisfy disclosure rules.
